solution:
The test is the one given in section 15.2.3 : an addition polymer's repeating unit has the SAME elemental composition as its monomer and is built from a monomer containing a double bond, whereas a condensation polymer's repeating unit carries a linkage (ester, amide) formed with loss of a small molecule.

Addition polymers :

a. \(\mathrm{-(CH_2-CH(C_6H_5)-)_n}\) - polystyrene, from the vinyl monomer styrene \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH{=}CH_2}\). Only carbon and hydrogen, no linking group.

b. \(\mathrm{-(CH_2-CH{=}CH-CH_2)_n}\) - polybutadiene, from 1,3-butadiene. One double bond survives per repeating unit, which is the signature of diene addition polymerization.

Condensation polymers :

c. \(\mathrm{-(CO(CH_2)_4-CONH(CH_2)_6NH-)_n}\) - nylon 6,6, a polyamide. The \(\mathrm{-CO-NH-}\) amide link is formed from adipic acid and hexamethylenediamine with loss of water.

d. \(\mathrm{-(OCH_2-CH_2-O-CO-C_6H_4-CO-)_n}\) - terylene or PET, a polyester. The \(\mathrm{-CO-O-}\) ester link is formed from terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol with loss of water.

Section 15.3.5 a gives the manufacture of nylon 6,6 in two steps.

Step 1 - salt formation. Adipic acid and hexamethylenediamine are mixed; the acid protonates the diamine and the nylon salt, hexamethylene diammonium adipate, separates :

\(\mathrm{HOOC-(CH_2)_4-COOH} + \mathrm{H_2N-(CH_2)_6-NH_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{{}^{-}O-CO-(CH_2)_4-CO-O^{-}}\ \mathrm{{}^{+}H_3N-(CH_2)_6-NH_3^{+}}\)

Step 2 - condensation polymerization. The nylon salt is heated to about 553 K under high pressure; each \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) condenses with an \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\), water is eliminated and the amide link is formed :

\(n\,(\text{nylon salt}) \xrightarrow[-n\mathrm{H_2O}]{553\ \mathrm{K},\ \text{high pressure}} \mathrm{[CO-(CH_2)_4-CO-NH-(CH_2)_6-NH]_n}\)

The product is the polyamide fibre nylon 6,6; the two numerals stand for the six carbon atoms in each of the two bifunctional monomers.

[Textbook note (not an error): part b asks which vulcanizing agent is used for Buna-N, and the chapter never states one. It gives sulfur for natural rubber (section 15.3.1) and for Buna-S (section 15.3.8), and magnesium oxide for neoprene (section 15.3.9 and Fig. 15.6 b), but Table 15.1 introduces Buna-N only as the butadiene-acrylonitrile copolymer and says nothing about vulcanising it. The model answer states the gap and marks the sulfur answer as an inference by analogy with Buna-S rather than as something the chapter says.]

Vulcanisation (section 15.3.1) is the process by which a network of cross links is introduced into an elastomer. Raw natural rubber is soft, has low tensile strength and consists of coiled polyisoprene chains held together only by weak van der Waals forces. Heating it with sulfur powder in presence of accelerators (the chapter names ZBX, zinc butyl xanthate) at about \(150\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) opens some of the \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\) double bonds, and one or more sulfur atoms then bridge two neighbouring chains. The result is a three dimensional cross linked network whose tensile strength, stiffness, elasticity and toughness are far higher than those of raw rubber; the cross links are also what pull the stretched rubber back to its original shape. Raising the sulfur content to 40-45% cross links the material so heavily that a hard, non-elastic solid, ebonite, is obtained.

a. Neoprene - the vulcanizing agent is **magnesium oxide, MgO**. Section 15.3.9 and Fig. 15.6 (b) show two neoprene chains treated with MgO and joined by an \(\mathrm{-O-}\) bridge in place of the chlorine atoms.

b. Buna-N - this chapter states NO vulcanizing agent for Buna-N anywhere. It gives sulfur for natural rubber and for Buna-S (section 15.3.8), and magnesium oxide for neoprene, while Table 15.1 lists Buna-N only as the butadiene-acrylonitrile copolymer. Buna-N retains one \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\) double bond per butadiene unit exactly as Buna-S does, so by analogy with the chapter's own treatment of Buna-S it would be vulcanised with sulfur; that is an inference from the chapter, not a statement made in it.

1) Teflon (section 15.3.3). Tetrafluoroethylene, a gas at room temperature, is polymerised at high pressure using a free radical initiator such as hydrogen peroxide or ammonium persulphate. This is addition polymerization, so no small molecule is lost :

\(n\,\mathrm{CF_2{=}CF_2} \xrightarrow[\text{peroxide}]{\text{polymerization}} \mathrm{[CF_2-CF_2]_n}\)

2) Bakelite (section 15.3.7 a and Fig. 15.3). It is formed in three stages.

Stage 1 : phenol and formaldehyde react over an acid or base catalyst to give hydroxymethyl phenols - the ortho and para mono-substituted products and the disubstituted product :

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + \mathrm{CH_2O} \xrightarrow{\text{acid or base}} \mathrm{HO-C_6H_4-CH_2OH}\)

Stage 2 : these condense with one another under \(\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}\), losing water at each step, and the phenol rings become linked through \(\mathrm{-CH_2-}\) bridges to give the linear moulding powder novolac :

\(n\,\mathrm{HO-C_6H_4-CH_2OH} \xrightarrow[-n\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}} \text{novolac}\)

Stage 3 : novolac is placed in a mould and heated at \(138\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) to \(176\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) under high pressure. Further \(\mathrm{-CH_2-}\) bridges form at the remaining free ortho and para positions, cross linking the chains into a rigid three dimensional network - bakelite, which is insoluble, infusible and of high tensile strength.

LDP is low density polyethylene and HDP is high density polyethylene; both are polythene, \(\mathrm{[CH_2-CH_2]_n}\), and section 15.3.2 states that polythene is of these two kinds.

| | LDP | HDP |
|---|---|---|
| Conditions of manufacture | Ethylene under high pressure, 1000-2000 atm, at 350-570 K with traces of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) or a peroxide as initiator | Ethene at only 6-7 atm and 333-343 K over a Ziegler-Natta catalyst (triethyl aluminium with titanium tetrachloride) |
| Mechanism | Free radical addition WITH H-atom abstraction, which introduces branching | No H-atom abstraction, so the chain grows essentially linear |
| Chain structure | Branched chains, loosely held, so the polymer has low density | Linear chains that pack closely, so the density is high and the polymer is crystalline |
| Properties | Extremely flexible but tough, chemically inert, moisture resistant, poor conductor of electricity, melting point \(110\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) | Much stiffer than LDP, high tensile strength and hardness, more resistant to chemicals, melting point 144-\(150\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) |
| Uses | Pipes for agriculture and irrigation, domestic water lines, insulation of electric and submarine cables, extruded films and sheets for packaging, squeeze bottles | Toys and household articles such as buckets, dustbins, bottles and pipes; laboratory ware and objects needing high tensile strength and stiffness |

The basic difference is therefore one of chain structure : branching in LDP keeps the chains apart and gives a soft, low density, flexible material, while the unbranched chains of HDP pack closely and give a stiff, dense, high strength material.

Preparation (section 15.3.3). Chemically teflon is polytetrafluoroethylene. Its monomer is tetrafluoroethylene, \(\mathrm{CF_2{=}CF_2}\), a gas at room temperature. It is polymerised at high pressure using free radical initiators such as hydrogen peroxide or ammonium persulphate :

\(n\,\mathrm{CF_2{=}CF_2} \xrightarrow[\text{peroxide}]{\text{polymerization}} \mathrm{[CF_2-CF_2]_n}\)

Properties. Teflon is tough, chemically inert and resistant to heat and to attack by corrosive reagents. The reason given is that the C-F bond is very difficult to break, so the polymer remains unaffected by corrosive alkali and by organic solvents.

Uses. It is used in making non-stick cookware, oil seals and gaskets.

Section 15.2.2 classifies polymers by chain configuration into linear (straight chain), branched chain and cross linked, and says that which one is obtained depends on the nature and number of functional groups in the monomer.

a. \(\mathrm{-(CH_2-CH(CN)-)_n}\) is **straight chain (linear)**. It is polyacrylonitrile, made from the bifunctional vinyl monomer acrylonitrile \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CHCN}\); the \(\mathrm{-CN}\) group is a pendant substituent on the backbone, not a branch of the chain, so the monomer units are joined in a single linear arrangement.

b. \(\mathrm{-(CH_2-CH_2-CH(CH_2-CH_2-)-CH_2-CH_2-)_n}\) is **branched chain**. A second \(\mathrm{-CH_2-CH_2-}\) chain grows sideways out of the backbone at the substituted carbon, which is exactly the arrangement section 15.2.2 b describes and which low density polythene has.

c. The structure in the figure, bakelite, is **cross linked**. Each phenol ring is joined through \(\mathrm{-CH_2-}\) bridges to neighbours in more than one direction, so the separate chains are tied to one another and the whole mass is a single three dimensional network. Section 15.2.2 c gives bakelite as its example of a cross linked polymer, and section 15.3.7 explains that these cross links are what make bakelite rigid, insoluble and infusible.

Polythene is manufactured by the addition polymerization of ethylene, in two ways that give the two kinds described in section 15.3.2.

Low density polythene (LDP) : ethylene is polymerised under high pressure, 1000-2000 atm, at 350-570 K in presence of traces of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) or a peroxide as initiator. The mechanism is free radical addition accompanied by H-atom abstraction, and it is that abstraction which introduces branching.

High density polythene (HDP) : ethene is polymerised at 333-343 K and only 6-7 atm in presence of a Ziegler-Natta catalyst, a combination of triethyl aluminium with titanium tetrachloride. The product is essentially a linear polymer.

In both cases : \(n\,\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{[CH_2-CH_2]_n}\)

Properties. LDP films are extremely flexible but tough, chemically inert and moisture resistant, a poor conductor of electricity, melting at \(110\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\). HDP is crystalline, melts at 144-\(150\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\), is much stiffer than LDP, has high tensile strength and hardness and is more resistant to chemicals.

Uses. LDP is used for pipes for agriculture, irrigation and domestic water lines, for insulation of electric and submarine cables, and for extruded films, sheets, squeeze bottles and packaging containers. HDP is used for toys and household articles such as buckets, dustbins, bottles and pipes, and for laboratory ware and other objects where high tensile strength and stiffness are required.

Yes. On the evidence this chapter gives, synthetic rubber is better than natural rubber in the following respects.

1. Mechanical strength and wear. Section 15.3.8 states outright that Buna-S is superior to natural rubber with regard to mechanical strength and that it has abrasion resistance, which is why it is used in the tyre industry. Raw natural rubber, by contrast, has to be vulcanised before its tensile strength, stiffness and toughness are acceptable (section 15.3.1).

2. Chemical and thermal resistance. Section 15.3.9 states that neoprene is particularly resistant to petroleum, vegetable oils, light and heat. That is why it is chosen for hose pipes carrying gasoline, for gaskets, and for insulator cable jackets and power transmission belts - services in which natural rubber would be attacked by the oil.

3. Control of properties. A synthetic rubber is made from chosen monomers in chosen proportions - Buna-S from 75 parts butadiene and 25 parts styrene - so its properties can be adjusted, whereas natural rubber is whatever the latex of the Hevea tree yields.

4. Supply. Natural rubber has to be tapped from mature trees, coagulated from latex and processed (the Do you know box of section 15.3.1), while synthetic rubber can be manufactured on demand.

Natural rubber is not without merit - it is the reference elastomer of the chapter and, once vulcanised, is elastic and tough - but for strength, abrasion resistance and resistance to oils and heat the synthetic rubbers are the better material.

Buna-S (SBR, styrene-butadiene rubber), section 15.3.8. It is an elastomer that is a COPOLYMER, obtained from 75 parts of butadiene and 25 parts of styrene by addition polymerization brought about by the action of sodium, and it is vulcanized with sulfur. Its speciality is that it is superior to natural rubber in mechanical strength and has abrasion resistance, so it is the rubber of the tyre industry.

Neoprene, section 15.3.9. It is a synthetic rubber that is the addition polymer of chloroprene (2-chloro-1,3-butadiene), which polymerises rapidly in presence of oxygen, and it is vulcanized with magnesium oxide. Its speciality is chemical resistance : it is particularly resistant to petroleum, vegetable oils, light and heat. Hence it is used for hose pipes for the transport of gasoline, for gaskets, and for insulator cable jackets and belts used in power transmission and conveying.

In short, Buna-S is chosen for strength and abrasion resistance, neoprene for resistance to oils, light and heat.

Isoprene is 2-methyl-1,3-butadiene, the monomer of natural rubber (section 15.3.1) :

\(\mathrm{CH_2{=}C(CH_3)-CH{=}CH_2}\)

On addition polymerization it gives polyisoprene, that is natural rubber :

\(n\,\mathrm{CH_2{=}C(CH_3)-CH{=}CH_2} \xrightarrow{\text{polymerization}} \mathrm{-[CH_2-C(CH_3){=}CH-CH_2]_n-}\)

Both double bonds of the diene take part, and a new double bond appears between carbons 2 and 3 of each repeating unit. The chapter adds that this \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\) bond has the cis configuration in natural rubber, which gives the molecule its coiled structure, and that the number of monomer units varies from about 2000 to 5000.

Section 15.2.3 a states that the free radical mechanism is the most common in addition polymerisation and that it is a chain reaction of three distinct steps.

**Step 1 - Chain initiation.** The reaction is started by a free radical. An initiator (catalyst) such as benzoyl peroxide, acetyl peroxide or tert-butyl peroxide is used to produce it; the weak peroxide \(\mathrm{O-O}\) bond breaks homolytically. For acetyl peroxide the chapter shows the fragment losing carbon dioxide to give a methyl radical :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-O-O-CO-CH_3} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{CH_3-CO-O^{\bullet}} \xrightarrow{-\mathrm{CO_2}} \mathrm{CH_3^{\bullet}}\)

The free radical, written R, then attaches itself to the olefin, that is the vinyl monomer, and produces a NEW radical made of two parts, the attached radical and the monomer unit :

\(\mathrm{R^{\bullet}} + \mathrm{CH_2{=}CHY} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R-CH_2-CHY^{\bullet}}\)

**Step 2 - Chain propagation.** The new radical reacts with another molecule of the vinyl monomer to form a still bigger radical, which in turn reacts with a further monomer molecule. This sequence repeats very rapidly and leads to a high molecular mass radical :

\(\mathrm{R-CH_2-CHY^{\bullet}} + n\,\mathrm{CH_2{=}CHY} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R-(CH_2-CHY)_n-CH_2-CHY^{\bullet}}\)

**Step 3 - Chain termination.** At some stage the growth of the chain stops. Termination may occur by several processes; the chapter gives the combination of two growing chain radicals :

\(2\,\mathrm{R-(CH_2-CHY)_n-CH_2-CHY^{\bullet}} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R-(CH_2CHY)_{n+1}-(CHYCH_2)_{n+1}-R}\)

The product is the polymer. Because no small molecule is lost at any step, the repeating unit has the same elemental composition as the monomer, which is the defining feature of addition polymerization.
